1317.title: Put up thy sword
1317.hook: friendship across divides, and deep caution about war
1317.carry: peacemakers treat no one as an enemy
1317.howItsDone: Catholics take up Fratelli Tutti's call to social friendship through parish dialogue groups, interfaith and community gatherings, and peace work; Catholic teaching on war is set out in the Catechism, and Francis's caution about it is discussed alongside that teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Fratelli Tutti and the road to Jericho. Your line was all brothers and sisters.

Every election season, opposite yard signs go up on two neighboring lawns, and every season the two neighbors stop waving. They used to borrow each other's ladders. Now they check the street before stepping outside so they won't have to talk. Nothing violent has happened. Nobody has done anything wrong, exactly. But something between them has been switched off. Fratelli Tutti has a name for what was lost, and it's the second half of the letter's own subtitle: on fraternity and social friendship. Today, that phrase, and where Francis follows it, all the way to the hardest place, war.
screen: `OPPOSITE YARD SIGNS.` → `SOMETHING SWITCHED OFF.` → `FRATERNITY AND SOCIAL FRIENDSHIP.`

segments.voice: First, what it means. Friendship is usually private: the few people you choose. Social friendship, for Francis, is the same warmth stretched across a whole society. Not agreeing with everyone. Not even liking everyone. But refusing to treat anyone as an enemy by default, and staying at the table. Second, how it's built. Francis puts dialogue at the center: approaching, listening, looking at each other, trying to understand, finding common ground. He warns against the opposite, the feverish exchange of opinions online, where people talk past each other and only hear their own side. Real dialogue, he says, is slow, and it costs something. Third, the hard edge: war. The Catechism keeps the Church's long teaching that a nation may defend itself under strict conditions, the teaching called just war. Francis doesn't erase it, but he says that with today's weapons it's very hard to meet those old criteria, and he cries out: never again war. Some Catholics read this as a turn toward nonviolence; others read it as a warning within the old teaching. Both look to the same Gospel. Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." And on the night he's arrested, when a disciple draws a sword, Jesus says: "Put up again thy sword into its place." Fourth, the link. Put side by side, war looks like social friendship failing at the largest scale. Peace between nations starts small, with two neighbors and a ladder.
screen: `FRIENDSHIP STRETCHED ACROSS A SOCIETY.` · `BUILT BY SLOW, REAL DIALOGUE.` · `DEEP CAUTION ABOUT WAR.` · `PEACE STARTS SMALL.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THE PEACEMAKERS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you've drifted from over a difference, politics, faith, family history, a side taken in an argument, and don't rehearse the argument; remember instead one thing about them you genuinely respect, or one thing you once shared. Then think of one small, low-stakes step toward them: a question about their kids, a recipe, a game you both follow. If you pray, hold them before God; if you don't, simply wish them well.
Social friendship. Fratelli Tutti's name for friendship stretched across a whole society, built by dialogue, and the opposite of war. Today's word.
Your line: peacemakers treat no one as an enemy. Not agreeing, not even liking, just staying at the table. See you tomorrow.

1318.title: Migrants
1318.howItsDone: Catholic parishes and charities welcome and accompany migrants and refugees through legal aid, language classes, housing help and resettlement work, and the Church keeps a yearly World Day of Migrants and Refugees.

segments.voice: Yesterday, social friendship, and Francis's deep caution about war. Your line was social friendship.

A family leaves home by night. The father has been warned in a dream that a ruler wants to kill their child. They don't wait for morning. They take the baby and his mother and head for another country, Egypt, where they'll live as foreigners until it's safe to come back. That's Matthew's Gospel, and in Catholic art it's called the Flight into Egypt. For a time, the Holy Family were people on the move. Pope Francis has pointed to that family when speaking about migrants and refugees, and he boiled the Church's response down to four verbs.
screen: `A FAMILY LEAVES IN THE NIGHT.` → `THE FLIGHT INTO EGYPT.` → `FOUR VERBS.`

segments.voice: First, welcome. The door has to open before anything else can happen. Francis talks about safe and legal ways in, so that people aren't pushed into the hands of smugglers. Behind it is Jesus's own line in the Douay-Rheims, from the judgment scene in Matthew: "I was a stranger, and you took me in." Second, protect. Once someone has arrived, they're often at the mercy of others: employers who don't pay, landlords who exploit, people who take their papers. Protecting means defending their rights and safety, especially for children. Third, promote. Not just keeping people alive, but helping them flourish: work, language, school, the chance to use their gifts. A doctor driving a taxi for years is a loss for everyone. Fourth, integrate. Not swallowing people up so they forget where they came from, and not leaving them on a separate island. Francis describes a two-way process, where newcomers and the community that receives them both change and both are enriched. Now the balance, because the Catholic tradition holds two things together. The Catechism says that more prosperous nations are obliged, as far as they are able, to welcome the foreigner in search of security and a livelihood. It also says that political authorities may set legal conditions on immigration for the common good, and that immigrants are obliged to respect the laws and heritage of the country that receives them. Catholics argue, sometimes sharply, about where that balance falls. But the four verbs sit underneath the argument: whatever the policy, the person in front of you is a person.

If no one comes to mind, think of a local group that serves migrants, and what it might need. If you pray, pray for families on the move; if you don't, simply hold that one person in mind.

Your line: four verbs. Welcome, protect, promote and integrate, whatever the policy. Rest well.

1319.title: A new industrial revolution
1319.hook: Leo XIV says he took his name partly after Leo XIII, facing a new revolution in technology
1319.howItsDone: Catholic universities, dioceses and Vatican offices study the ethics of new technology and artificial intelligence in the light of social teaching, and Catholics discuss it in parish and workplace groups.

segments.voice: Yesterday, migrants, and Francis's four verbs: welcome, protect, promote, integrate. Your line was four verbs.

Why Leo? A new pope, speaking to the cardinals who had just elected him, explained the name he'd chosen. Because of an earlier Leo, Leo the Thirteenth, who wrote Rerum Novarum, a letter on the condition of workers, at a time when factories and machines were remaking how people worked and lived. That was an industrial revolution. Today, the new pope, Leo the Fourteenth, says, the Church faces another one: a revolution in technology, artificial intelligence among it, raising new questions about human dignity, justice and work. A name chosen as a signal.
screen: `A NEW POPE EXPLAINS HIS NAME.` → `LEO XIII AND THE FACTORIES.` → `ANOTHER REVOLUTION.`

segments.voice: First, the echo. Leo the Thirteenth described workers left isolated and helpless before hard employers and unchecked competition. He insisted that employers must not treat workers as slaves, or use people as things for profit. Leo the Fourteenth's point is that the same question has come back in new clothes. Second, the new machines. This time they don't only lift and weld. They sort, write, recommend and predict. They can help a doctor or a farmer. They can also replace a worker, track an employee's every minute, or decide what whole crowds of people see. Catholic social teaching doesn't treat technology as evil. It treats it as made by people, so it can be shaped by people, for people. Third, the measure. The tradition's test is simple to say and hard to keep: does this serve the human person, or does the person end up serving it? A good tool exists for people. When the order flips, something's gone wrong. Fourth, the old garden. In Genesis, God puts the first human in paradise "to dress it, and to keep it." Work and care, from the beginning. Not to be replaced, not to be used up, but to tend. That's the picture behind Leo the Fourteenth's signal: machines that help people tend the world, never people reduced to parts of a machine.
screen: `THE SAME QUESTION, NEW CLOTHES.` · `MACHINES THAT SORT, WRITE, PREDICT.` · `DOES IT SERVE THE PERSON?` · `TO DRESS IT, AND TO KEEP IT.` · then, large: `WORK AND CARE, FROM THE BEGINNING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the screen you use most and think about yesterday: when did it serve you, and when did you end up serving it, a scroll that ate an hour, a notification that pulled you from a face? Then pick one small change that puts the person first: the phone in another room at dinner, a real voice instead of a text, one app silenced. If you pray, offer that choice to God; if you don't, simply decide it, quietly.
A new industrial revolution. Leo the Fourteenth's name for the change technology is bringing, and the reason he looked back to Leo the Thirteenth. Today's word.
Your line: people before machines. A good tool exists for people. Until tomorrow.

1320.title: Trafficking (8 February)
1320.hook: on Bakhita's day the Church prays against human trafficking
1320.howItsDone: On 8 February, the feast of Saint Josephine Bakhita, Catholics keep a day of prayer and reflection against human trafficking, and religious sisters and Catholic charities run shelters, outreach and awareness work for survivors.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Leo the Fourteenth and a new industrial revolution. Your line was people before machines.

A little girl in Sudan, out in the fields near her village, is grabbed by strangers and carried off. She's so frightened that, by her own later account, she forgets the name her parents gave her. Her captors give her a new one: Bakhita. She is sold, and sold again, and she bears the scars. Years later, in Italy, she meets the Canossian sisters, is baptized Josephine, and stays among them for the rest of her life. This path met her last year. The Church keeps her feast on the eighth of February, and on that day it prays against the trade that took her childhood.
screen: `A GIRL TAKEN FROM THE FIELDS.` → `SOLD, AND SOLD AGAIN.` → `JOSEPHINE BAKHITA, 8 FEBRUARY.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Bakhita is an Arabic word meaning fortunate, or lucky. Her kidnappers gave it to her. It's hard to hear that without wincing: a stolen child called the lucky one. And yet Josephine Bakhita kept the name all her life, and the Church honors her by it. Second, the turn. In Italy, when the family that held her wanted to take her away again, the question of her freedom went before the authorities, and she was recognized as free. She chose to stay with the sisters, and later became one of them. Her story isn't only about what was done to her. It's about a woman who was owned and then, at last, belonged to herself, and gave herself to God. Third, the word today. Trafficking is the buying, selling, moving or holding of people by force, fraud or coercion, for labor, for sex, for profit. It isn't only a story from another century. It happens in fields and kitchens, on fishing boats, in nail salons and apartments, sometimes in plain sight. Fourth, the Church's response. On Bakhita's feast the Church keeps a day of prayer and reflection against trafficking, and religious sisters run shelters and outreach for survivors. Underneath is Jesus in the synagogue at Nazareth, where he reads from Isaiah that he has been sent "to preach deliverance to the captives." Catholic teaching holds that a person can never be property. Not for any price. Not for any reason.

segments.voice: Hold one sign that anti-trafficking groups often point to: someone not allowed to keep their own passport or ID, because a boss keeps it, or a worker who owes a debt they can never seem to pay off. You're not looking to accuse anyone; you're learning to see. If you pray, ask Saint Josephine Bakhita to pray for those held captive; if you don't, simply remember her name.

1321.title: Goods for all
1321.hook: private property is real, but the earth's goods are meant for everyone
1321.howItsDone: Catholics live out the universal destination of goods through almsgiving, parish sharing programs and food banks, lending and giving what sits unused, and, in religious orders, holding property in common.

segments.voice: Yesterday, trafficking, and Josephine Bakhita. Your line was no one for sale.

"The earth is the Lord's and the fulness thereof: the world, and all they that dwell therein." That's a psalm, in the Douay-Rheims. Now look around the room you're in. The chair is yours. The phone is yours. Maybe the walls are yours, or the bank's. Catholic teaching says those claims are real. You can own things, and nobody gets to just take them. But it also says that underneath every deed and receipt, there's an older claim, and it belongs to everyone. The Church has a long, slightly clunky name for it.
screen: `THE EARTH IS THE LORD'S.` → `THE CHAIR IS YOURS.` → `AN OLDER CLAIM UNDERNEATH.`

segments.voice: The name is the universal destination of goods. Destination here means purpose: where the goods of the earth are meant to go. First, the gift. The Catechism starts here: God entrusted the earth and its resources to the whole human race, to take care of them and enjoy their fruits. The land, the water, the harvest were a gift to everyone before they were anyone's. Second, property is real. The Church doesn't abolish ownership. The Catechism defends the right to private property: people need a measure of security, a home, the freedom to plan and provide for their families. Owning things, rightly used, is good. Third, the two hold together. The right to private property, the Catechism says, does not do away with the original gift of the earth to all. So what you own, you hold as a kind of steward. The Second Vatican Council puts it this way in Gaudium et Spes: a person should regard the things they lawfully possess as common in this sense, that they can benefit others as well as themselves. Fourth, the early Church, which this path first met in year one. In Acts, the believers in Jerusalem shared what they had, and the Douay-Rheims says that "all things were common unto them." Catholic teaching doesn't require everyone to live that way, though religious orders live something like it. But it stands as a picture of where the goods of the earth are headed. So the question isn't, is this mine? It usually is. The question is, what is this for?
screen: `THE EARTH: A GIFT TO EVERYONE.` · `PRIVATE PROPERTY IS REAL.` · `YOU HOLD IT AS A STEWARD.` · `ALL THINGS WERE COMMON.` · then, large: `WHAT IS THIS FOR?`

segments.voice: Go through your home in your mind, room by room, and notice what sits unused: a coat in the closet, tools in the garage, books on a shelf. No guilt; just ask of each thing, what is this for, then pick one you could lend or give, and one person or group who could use it. If you pray, thank God for what you have; if you don't, simply hold the thing and the person together.
Universal destination of goods. Private property is real, but the earth's goods are meant, in the end, to serve everyone. Today's word.
Your line: meant for all. Yours, and still meant to serve others too. Same time tomorrow.

1322.title: Nonviolence
1322.hook: a pope's peace message names active nonviolence as a way of life and of politics
1322.howItsDone: Catholics pray for peace at Mass and on the Church's World Day of Peace, and some Catholic groups train in nonviolent action; parish and family life is where the Church asks it to begin.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the universal destination of goods: what you own is truly yours, and the earth's goods are still meant for everyone. Your line was meant for all.

A kitchen, late at night, two people mid-argument. One voice rises. The other has a choice: rise to meet it, go cold and silent, or try something harder. Paul names that harder thing for the Christians in Rome, in the Douay-Rheims: "Be not overcome by evil: but overcome evil by good." Not run from it. Not match it. Overcome it, with its opposite. Pope Francis built a World Day of Peace message around one word, and carried it from kitchens like that one all the way into politics. Today, nonviolence.
screen: `A KITCHEN, A RAISED VOICE.` → `OVERCOME EVIL BY GOOD.` → `A POPE'S PEACE MESSAGE.`

segments.voice: Francis starts with the Sermon on the Mount. Jesus says to love your enemies, and in the Douay-Rheims, "do good to them that hate you." Francis reads that as a whole way of living: to be a true follower of Jesus today includes embracing his teaching about nonviolence. Then the word that matters most: active. Nonviolence isn't giving up, looking away, or letting a bully win. It's a choice to resist evil without copying it. Francis names people who did exactly that and changed things, among them Mother Teresa and Martin Luther King. It takes courage, planning and nerve. It can stand in a street. Where does it begin? Not first at a border or a parliament. At home, Francis says, in families, where people learn to argue without wounding and to forgive without pretending nothing happened. A kitchen table is a peace table too. And an honest note. The Catechism still keeps a place for legitimate defense, and Catholic teaching thinks hard about when force can be just. Francis doesn't erase that. He asks that nonviolence become the first instinct and the normal style, in private life and in politics, with force a last and sorrowful exception. Two strands, held in one Church. Up close, it looks small: an angry reply left unsent, a voice lowered, standing beside someone instead of against them.
screen: `LOVE YOUR ENEMIES, DO THEM GOOD.` · `ACTIVE, NOT PASSIVE.` · `IT STARTS AT HOME.` · `DEFENSE STILL HAS A PLACE.` · then, large: `OVERCOME EVIL BY GOOD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one conflict you're in right now, with a coworker, a sibling, a neighbor, a thread online, and notice what you're holding ready: the sharp line you've rehearsed, the silence meant to punish. Without giving up what's true, find the gentler move, a question instead of a verdict, and breathe with it. If you pray, bring that person before God by name.
Nonviolence. Resisting evil without copying it: in Francis's message, a style for home and for politics, rooted in the Sermon on the Mount.
Your line: active nonviolence. Not passive, not violent: overcome evil by good. See you tomorrow.

1323.title: Caritas
1323.hook: the Church's charity agencies carry the word caritas, love, to the ends of the earth
1323.howItsDone: Catholics give to charity through parish collections, diocesan appeals and agencies such as Caritas, Catholic Charities and Catholic Relief Services, and some parishes run food pantries and volunteer programs of their own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nonviolence, and Paul's line about overcoming evil with good. Your line was active nonviolence.

A flood comes through a town, and a few days later a truck pulls up with water, blankets and people in vests. A refugee family lands in a strange city, and someone meets them with a key to an apartment. A man leaves prison with nowhere to go, and a desk somewhere has his name on a list. Look at the logo on the vest or the door, and often enough it says Caritas, or Catholic Charities, or Catholic Relief Services. One Latin word sits behind all of them.
screen: `A FLOOD, A TRUCK, A BLANKET.` → `A KEY FOR A NEW FAMILY.` → `ONE LATIN WORD.`

segments.voice: You met this word back on day two hundred ninety-six: God is charity. Caritas is the Latin the Church uses for love, the self-giving kind, and older English Bibles render it charity. Paul describes it to the Corinthians, in the Douay-Rheims: "Charity is patient, is kind." So charity, first, isn't a donation. It's a way of loving. Then a decision in Acts. The first Christians in Jerusalem share food with widows every day, and a complaint goes up: some widows are being missed. The apostles don't shrug, and they don't drop everything else. They choose seven men to take charge of the daily serving, so no one is skipped. Pope Benedict the Sixteenth, in his letter God is Love, points to that moment: from then on, serving the poor is organized, and it's part of who the Church is. Then his big claim. The Church can't do without three things: proclaiming the word, celebrating the sacraments, and the service of charity. Take one away and something essential is missing. Charity isn't an extra for spare time. And what that grew into: some parishes run food pantries, dioceses run charities, and Catholic agencies work across borders, joined in a confederation called Caritas Internationalis. Benedict adds one warning. The people who serve need hearts formed by love, not just training, so that a person in need meets a person, not a process. A blanket handed over coldly is still a blanket. Handed over with love, it's caritas.
screen: `CARITAS: LOVE THAT GIVES ITSELF.` · `SEVEN CHOSEN TO SERVE TABLES.` · `WORD, SACRAMENT, CHARITY.` · `A PERSON, NOT A PROCESS.` · then, large: `CHARITY IS PATIENT, IS KIND.`

segments.voice: If you're able, choose one group that serves people in need, near or far, and give it something, money, an hour, a bag of clothes, any size at all. Then bring to mind one person it might reach, someone you'll never meet, and hold them for a few breaths. If you pray, offer the gift and the person to God.
Caritas. Latin for the love that gives itself. This week's road: social friendship, four verbs, people before machines, no one for sale, meant for all, active nonviolence, and now charity everywhere.
Your line: charity everywhere. A name on a van or a door, and a love underneath it. Rest well.
